title: Flame spread: Effects of microgravity and scale
text: and long enough to allow for unrestricted growth. Differences between ﬂame spread in purely buoyant and purely forced ﬂows are presented. Prior to these experiments, only samples of small size in small conﬁned volumes had been tested in space. Therefore the ﬁrst and third ﬂights in the experimen- tal series, called “Saﬃre,” studied large-scale ﬂame spread over a 94 cm long by 40.6 cm wide cotton- ﬁberglass fabric. The second ﬂight examined an array of nine smaller samples of various materials each measuring 29 cm long by 5 cm wide. Among them were two of the same cotton-ﬁberglass fabric used in the large-scale tests and a thick, ﬂat PMMA sample (1-cm thick). The forced airﬂow was 20–25 cm/s, which is typical of air circulation speeds in a spacecraft. The experiments took place aboard the Cygnus vehicle, a large unmanned resupply spacecraft to the International Space Station (ISS). The experiments were carried out in orbit before the Cygnus vehicle, reloaded with ISS trash, re-entered the Earth’s atmo- sphere and perished. The downloaded test data show that a concurrent (downstream) spreading ﬂame over thin fabrics in microgravity reaches a steady spread rate and a limiting length. The ﬂame over the thick PMMA sample approaches a non-growing, steady state in the 15 min burning duration and has a limiting pyrolysis length. In contrast, upward (concurrent) ﬂame spread at normal gravity on Earth is usu- ally found to be accelerating so that the ﬂame size grows with time. The existence of a ﬂame size limit has important considerations for spacecraft ﬁre safety as it can be used to establish the heat release rate in the vehicle. The ﬁndings and the scientiﬁc explanations of this series of innovative, novel and unique experiments are presented, analyzed and discussed. © 2018 The Combustion Institute. Right: concurrent spread in forced ﬂow inside a ﬂow tunnel. include gas-phase ﬂow time, diffusion time, chemical time and the solid heat-up and conduction times. All of these are affected by the types and magnitudes of oxidizer ﬂows. Furthermore, the inﬂu- ences of some of these parameters on ﬂame spread are profoundly affected by gravity-induced buoyant ﬂows. Oxygen is drawn into the ﬂame reaction zone as combustion products are transported away in the buoyant plume. As illustrated in the left part of Fig. 1 , this buoyant ﬂow can be acceleratory along an upwardly spread- ing ﬂame. Starting at the base of the ﬂame with a very modest magnitude, the ﬂow accelerates upward as the size of the ﬂame increases, and in extreme cases can reach velocities of several tens of meters per second [5] . This buoyant ﬂow affects the mass ﬂow rate of both oxygen and fuel at the ﬂame location, the chemical re- action rate at the ﬂame, and the heat transfer rate from the ﬂame to the fuel surface, which in turn will govern the ﬂame stabil- ity and its spread rate. In the absence of gravity, a ﬂame would spread by diffusion of heat and mass in a quiescent oxidizer, or by forced convection if there are externally induced gaseous ﬂows near the fuel surface. Although the basic mechanisms of ﬂame spread are the same with or without gravity, the relative magni- tudes and characteristics of the transport of heat and mass and the ﬂame chemical kinetics may be different, which may cause differ- ent types of ﬂame spread. Although the basic mechanisms of ﬂame spread are the same with or without gravity, the relative magni- tudes and characteristics of the transport of heat and mass and the ﬂame chemical kinetics may be different, which may cause differ- ent types of ﬂame spread. In the absence of gravity, ﬂame spread behavior is not entirely resolved. Aboard an orbiting spacecraft such as the International Space Station (ISS), gravitational forces are miniscule. As a result, a ﬂame aboard the ISS cannot generate any signiﬁcant buoyant con- vective ﬂow. However, a slow forced ﬂow is present because of ventilation (about 10–20 cm/s). Natural convective ﬂow and forced ﬂow differ in both their detailed structure near burning surfaces and their development along those surfaces, as shown for concur- rent ﬂame spread in Fig. 1 . Moreover, the magnitude of this forced ﬂow aboard spacecraft is much smaller than the peak buoyant ﬂow induced by ﬂames in normal gravity (between 0.3 m/s at the ﬂame base to several m/s downstream). Given the differences in the con- vective ﬂows, the response of the ﬂame in these two environments remains a central question. In normal gravity, an upward spreading ﬂame usually grows and accelerates. Will this happen in micro- gravity when a ﬂame is only exposed to a forced convective ﬂow? How large can a ﬁre become in microgravity? How do ﬂammabil- ity and ﬂame stability change? In addition to these fundamental scientiﬁc questions, there are very practical safety concerns since there are limited escape options from a spacecraft. Unfortunately, because of ﬂame-induced buoyancy, it is very diﬃcult to reproduce on Earth the environmental conditions of a spacecraft, particularly the low velocity ﬂows. Consequently, ﬁre testing of materials to be used in spacecraft requires extrapolations of normal gravity tests (with certain assumptions), utilization of reduced gravity facilities, or alternative approaches to diminish the effects buoyancy. While it is challenging to perform large-scale combustion experiments aboard orbiting platforms, the results provide a crucial connection between 1-g tests, small-scale microgravity experiments, and the- ory. 1.1. Experimental background Over the years, the combustion and ﬁre research community, led by NASA, has conducted microgravity experiments on ﬂame spread and growth over solids in microgravity. The tests conducted using ground–based facilities such as drop towers [6–8] and air- planes ﬂying parabolic trajectories [9,10] were limited by the short microgravity test duration, while past space experiments were lim- ited to small samples due to safety considerations on the Inter- national Space Station. For example, in the recent BASS (Burning and Suppression of Solids) project on the ISS [11] , ﬂame spread experiments were carried out in a small ﬂow tunnel using cotton- ﬁberglass fabric samples measuring only 2.1 cm x 10 cm. One of the main ﬁndings of solid burning in microgravity is that gaseous and surface radiation are important in low-intensity ﬂames typical of those near extinction [12–14] . In previous normal gravity work, radiation in ﬁres was considered an important mech- anism for ﬂame development only when the ﬂame size became greater than about 40 cm, at which point these large ﬂames yielded substantial soot radiation [15] . In microgravity, radiation (net loss from the surface and gas phase) becomes comparatively more im- portant, not because the radiative ﬂux increases, but rather be- cause of the absence of natural convection. When the convective velocity decreases, the ratio of radiative loss rate to the heat gen- eration rate increases, so the ﬂame temperature decreases and ra- diative losses alone, from the ﬂame’s gas-phase ﬁeld and from the fuel surface, are suﬃcient to lead to ﬂame quenching [12] . This has a large impact on key ﬂame phenomena such as ignition, ﬂame spread, and extinction [16] . In many low-speed microgravity exper- iments, the small ﬂames near the extinction limit have no visible

Urban et al. / Combustion and Flame 199 (2019) 168–182 In addition to the magnitude of the ﬂow velocity, the direction of ﬂame spread with respect to the direction of ﬂow is impor- tant [17,18] . Opposed ﬂame spread occurs when the two directions are against each other (e.g. downward spread in buoyant ﬂow and upstream spread in forced ﬂow). Concurrent ﬂame spread occurs when the two directions are the same (upward spread in buoyant ﬂow and downstream spread in forced ﬂow). In opposed spread, the controlling zones for ﬂame spread and stabilization are collo- cated at the ﬂame base. Assuming that upstream gas-phase con- duction is the dominant heat transfer mode, the size of this region is given by the thermal length α/U where α is the gas thermal dif- fusivity and U is the ﬂow speed in this zone. While the thermal length scale is typically very small, it controls ﬂame stabilization and forward heat conduction. Because the heat ﬂux and the pre- heat length have the opposite dependence on this length scale, a canceling effect renders the spread of ﬂames over a thin fuel in opposed ﬂow relatively insensitive to the air speed except near the blow-off limit [3,19–21] . For a thick fuel, however, the ratio of the forward gas phase conduction and the heat conduction into the solid renders opposed-ﬂow ﬂame spread dependent on the ﬂow speed [3,19–21] . In addition, gas phase chemical kinetics may af- fect the spread rate and even cause extinction (blow-off) of the ﬂame at high ﬂow speed [3,22] . At very-low-ﬂow speeds in mi- crogravity, radiation heat losses and chemical kinetic effects may also cause extinction (quenching) of the ﬂame [12,23–26] . Thus, although in purely-forced-ﬂow opposed spread, the downstream ﬂame size (e.g. ﬂame length) does not affect the spread rate sig- niﬁcantly, in the presence of gravity the induced ﬂow velocity will increase as the ﬂame becomes larger affecting both the heat trans- fer from the ﬂame to the solid and the gas phase chemical kinetics. In concurrent-ﬂow ﬂame spread, the controlling zones for ﬂame spread

text: spread, the downstream ﬂame size (e.g. ﬂame length) does not affect the spread rate sig- niﬁcantly, in the presence of gravity the induced ﬂow velocity will increase as the ﬂame becomes larger affecting both the heat trans- fer from the ﬂame to the solid and the gas phase chemical kinetics. In concurrent-ﬂow ﬂame spread, the controlling zones for ﬂame spread and stabilization are separate and distinct [17,18] . Flame spread depends on the length of the ﬂame and its thermal plume, an important distinction compared to the opposed-ﬂow case which normally depends only on the thermal length scale. In typical concurrent-ﬂow, ﬂame spread conﬁgurations (includ- ing upward spread in normal gravity and forced ﬂow at elevated air velocity), the solid preheating and pyrolysis rates are domi- nated by convection, and the external ﬂow velocity will therefore inﬂuence both the ﬂame length and the heat ﬂux from the ﬂame to the solid surface [3,27–29] . Since there are marked differences in the velocity distributions between a buoyant-induced ﬂow on Earth and a purely-forced ﬂow in microgravity, it is expected that there will be notable differences in ﬂame spread in buoyant and forced ﬂows. In upward spread over a solid surface, for example, the buoyant induced ﬂow starts to accelerate from the ﬂame base until it is balanced by viscous drag caused by the solid surface. This ﬂow acceleration entrains oxygen into the ﬂame. The pyrolysis rate and consequently the ﬂame length increase with ﬂow velocity, so therefore an incipient ﬂame spread may continually grow from the point of ignition [30–33] . Also, concurrent-ﬂow ﬂame spread de- pends on fuel thickness because of the requirements to heat and pyrolyze the solid. In turn, the fuel vapor which is generated in the pyrolysis region controls ﬂame length. When the fuel is thick it may not readily burn out and consequently the ﬂame length can increase as the ﬂame spreads. However, the ﬂame standoff distance also increases and as a result the convective heat ﬂux from the ﬂame to the solid is reduced. The relationship between these two effects determines whether the ﬂame spread

text: region controls ﬂame length. When the fuel is thick it may not readily burn out and consequently the ﬂame length can increase as the ﬂame spreads. However, the ﬂame standoff distance also increases and as a result the convective heat ﬂux from the ﬂame to the solid is reduced. The relationship between these two effects determines whether the ﬂame spread rate will increase or remain constant [27,34] . When the fuel is thin, however, the burning region may slowly lengthen or remain constant due to fuel burn-out, and the ﬂame spread rate may become constant regardless of whether the ﬂame is in a natural convection [35] or forced ﬂow [36] environment. Some investigations have shown that an upward-burning ﬂame over thin narrow paper samples in reduced pressure could reach a steady rate and with a constant (limiting) ﬂame length [28,37] . This means that the sample burnout rate was equal to the pyroly- sis advance rate. It should be noted that as pressure is reduced, the buoyant ﬂow velocity and its effect on the ﬂame spread rate are reduced; and the ﬂame standoff distance from the solid surface in- creases. In an experiment of ﬂow-assisted horizontal spread burn- ing paper samples in a wind tunnel in normal gravity [36] , it was also found that pyrolysis front spread rate became constant once the pyrolysis length reached a steady value. In this case, the hor- izontal conﬁguration limited buoyant effects on the ﬂame spread rate. Apart from these exceptions (when the ﬂame reaches a lim- iting length), most reasonable-scale experiments suggest upward ﬂame spread on Earth is a continuous growth process. This raises the natural question: Will concurrent ﬂame spread in purely-forced ﬂow follow the same trend? The answer has important practical implications for spacecraft ﬁre safety as it inﬂuences how large of a heat release rate can be tolerated in a spacecraft. Up until this cur- rent research effort, there were no opportunities to perform large- scale combustion experiments in microgravity. Up until this cur- rent research effort, there were no opportunities to perform large- scale combustion experiments in microgravity. Early spacecraft ﬁre safety approaches were instead based solely on the results of 1- g testing and extrapolations from small-scale, low-gravity testing. Consequently, spacecraft ﬁre safety protocols and procedures car- ried a level of risk that could not be quantiﬁed. 1.2. Theoretical background To help better understand the pertinent issues for the current work, a brief description of the theoretical background is pre- sented. First, a simpliﬁed thermal theory based on heat transfer considerations in the preheat zone of the spreading ﬂame over a thin solid is introduced. Then, the detailed numerical model is de- scribed. As the large-scale fuel used in this study burned as a thin ma- terial, and ﬂame spread in a concurrent ﬂow is the primary form of burning, the discussion in this section will focus on concurrent ﬂame spread for thin fuels. In this mode of ﬂame spread the oxi- dizing gas ﬂows by convection (forced, free, or mixed) in the same direction as that of the ﬂame propagation ( Fig. 1 ). The reacting gases (hot) and post-combustion gases generated in the pyrolysis region move ahead of the pyrolysis front in the form of a ﬂame transferring heat to the virgin fuel downstream. Because the py- rolyzed fuel and oxidizer are initially separated, the ﬂame is pri- marily of the diffusion type, and its characteristics are those of a boundary layer diffusion ﬂame [38] that extends beyond the burn- ing region. Because of its diffusion characteristics the ﬂame is not strongly affected by ﬁnite-rate chemical kinetics, except under lim- iting conditions such as low oxygen concentration, low pressure, very low ﬂow velocity that may quench the ﬂame, or high ﬂow velocity that may affect the upstream leading edge of the ﬂame where extinction will ﬁrst occur (blow-off). Thus, except in limit- ing conditions, the spread of the ﬂame will be controlled primarily by

title: Flame spread: Effects of microgravity and scale
text: ﬁnite-rate chemical kinetics, except under lim- iting conditions such as low oxygen concentration, low pressure, very low ﬂow velocity that may quench the ﬂame, or high ﬂow velocity that may affect the upstream leading edge of the ﬂame where extinction will ﬁrst occur (blow-off). Thus, except in limit- ing conditions, the spread of the ﬂame will be controlled primarily by the rate of heat transfer from the downstream ﬂame to the vir- gin fuel ahead of the pyrolysis front. The length of the ﬂame is determined by the fuel pyrolysis rate and the burning rate of the pyrolyzate and oxidizer. For thin samples, the fuel may burn out in the upstream region of the fuel, which in turn affects the length of the pyrolysis region. This length, i.e., the pyrolysis length, will depend on the relative magnitudes of the ﬂame spread and fuel regression rates [38] . The early theoretical models of concurrent ﬂame spread over thin fuels were primarily heat transfer analyses with the ﬂame spread rate obtained from the solution of the solid phase energy equation. The heat ﬂux at the fuel surface was obtained from the solution of the combustion laminar boundary layer for a non- radiative ﬂame [27,39] or from experimental measurements [29] .

Based on the characteristics of laminar bound- ary layer ﬂames, the models predict an increasing spread rate for upward buoyant ﬂow [31] but a constant spread rate for purely- forced ﬂow [36,39] . These predictions follow from considerations of the heat ﬂux on the solid surface as determined by the ﬂame standoff distance, temperature, and length. In laminar upward free ﬂow the length of the ﬂame dominates the decrease of the heat ﬂux with distance. However, in forced ﬂow both effects cancel each other. Regarding the effect of the forced ﬂow velocity, forced ﬂow models [27,40,41] predict a spread rate that increases with the ﬂow velocity, although experimentally it becomes constant at relatively large velocities [34] . Another analytical approach to model the concurrent-ﬂow case is to view it as an ignition problem with ﬂame spread rate calcu- lated as the ratio of a heating length (ﬂame length) to an ignition time [1–4,20] . The ﬁrst thing to note is that in normal Earth gravity it is not possible to observe forced- ﬂow ﬂame spread, because, in order to overcome gravity effects, the ﬂow velocity, U f , would have to be so large that the ﬂame would be extinguished by blow-off. In microgravity, as in the ex- periments reported here, the concurrent ﬂame spread rate would have the form V f ∝ P 1 / 2 l 1 / 2 p U 1 / 2 f  T f −T p  (6) The predicted dependence of the spread rate on the ﬂow ve- locity is somewhere between a one-half power and linear, depend- ing on the dependence of the pyrolysis length on the ﬂow veloc- ity. Also, since initially the pyrolysis length increases with time, the predicted spread rate also increases with time. However, as the ﬂame spreads over the solid surface the pyrolysis length may become constant [35,36] , in which case Eq. (5) would predict a constant spread rate. Although this seems to agree with the ex- periments of Markstein and de Ris [35] , their sample tested may not have been long enough to verify this result rigorously. In ad- dition, it should be kept in mind that Eq. (4) holds for laminar ﬂow, whereas for turbulent ﬂow, Eq. (5) would show different de- pendences on the problem parameters. Also, the ﬂame tempera- ture would be affected by turbulence and ﬂow oxygen concentra- tion. Such dependences do not seem straightforward as shown in earlier experiments [45] . It is clear that the scale of the fuel sam- ple to be tested is an important consideration to draw conclusions about the burning of a material because the sample size will affect the variation with time of the pyrolysis length, the transition from laminar to turbulent ﬂow, and other ﬂame characteristics (temper- ature, soot, and radiation). The simple analytical expression for ﬂame spread rate given by Eq. (6) reveals useful physical insight. To go beyond its limi- tations, some of the simplifying assumptions used in its derivation can be removed by developing a more detailed numerical model, from which results are presented later. Still, it is instructive to re- view ﬁrst several previous works from which the present model has evolved. The focus will be on ﬂame spread in concurrent ﬂows, especially in the low ﬂow velocity regime, and for thin solids. The model objectives are to address several questions, includ- ing: What are the roles of radiation on ﬂame spread and stabiliza- tion? What is the spatial distribution of fuel pyrolysis rate under the ﬂame? What are the differences in ﬂame spread comparing purely-buoyant and purely-forced ﬂows? (Note that in using an av- eraged h and U m , the details of the buoyant and forced ﬂow ﬁelds cannot be readily addressed by Eq. (4) ). Can the dependence of py- rolysis length (or preheating length) on ﬂow velocity or gravity be determined? Will pyrolysis length reach a constant value for long samples, and does fuel thickness play a role? What are the signiﬁ- cant three-dimensional features of ﬂame spread over narrow sam- ples? How does an upstream boundary layer affect ﬂame spread?

Urban et al. / Combustion and Flame 199 (2019) 168–182 Motivated by an experiment [37] where steady, upward ﬂame spread was observed over narrow paper samples in reduced pressure, a modeling effort [40] was initiated to look for steady solutions over thin solids. The two dimensional model examined low-speed forced ﬂow, which is more relevant for microgravity ap- plications. In order to speed up the computation, steady equations were discretized and iteratively solved, with the ﬂame spread rate being an eigenvalue to the problem. The steady formulation neces- sitated assuming complete fuel burnout, because any leftover inert material would be left behind (see the right part of Fig. 1 ) and the ﬂame would effectively move into an ever-thickening bound- ary layer making a steady solution intractable. Hence the model assumes no inert in the fuel and a one-step, zeroth-order py- rolysis reaction so the solid can burn out completely. A ﬂame- ﬁxed coordinate system effectively pins the ﬂame in the domain, facilitating a steady formulation, and a ﬁnite-rate, gas-phase reac- tion is included to address the ﬂame stability and extinction ques- tion. This requires an elliptic description and the use of Navier– Stokes equation [46] in the ﬂame base zone. Because the size of this zone varies with ﬂow velocity, a non-dimensional grid is used in the numerical solution to assure ﬂame structure resolution. It is essential to determine the local solid burning rate at the ﬂame base since the solid burning rate is the highest there. For a short ﬂame in low-speed forced ﬂow, a large portion of the pyrolysis fuel mass is ejected at the ﬂame base, which in turn controls the ﬂame length. The model [40] predicts steady spread with a constant lim- iting length for wide (2-D) sample. The predicted pyrolysis length is found to be proportional to ﬂow speed, and the steady ﬂame spread rate is also proportional to the ﬂow speed, consistent with the expression in Eq. (6) . This early model includes only surface radiation loss and not ﬂame radiation. A follow-up two-dimensional model [41] added the contribution from gas-phase

The predicted pyrolysis length is found to be proportional to ﬂow speed, and the steady ﬂame spread rate is also proportional to the ﬂow speed, consistent with the expression in Eq. (6) . This early model includes only surface radiation loss and not ﬂame radiation. A follow-up two-dimensional model [41] added the contribution from gas-phase radiation from CO 2 and H 2 O by solving the discrete ordinate radiation transfer equation. The model was applied to both low-speed forced ﬂow and low-gravity buoy- ant ﬂow. Again, iteration was used to obtain steady solutions. Com- pared with the aforementioned results [40] , gas radiation modi- ﬁes the ﬂame length, spread rate and ﬂame extinction limit. These quantities are found to be very sensitive to both the gas and the solid radiation. In the forced-ﬂow computation, ﬂame length in- creases when radiation losses are reduced. When both gas and surface radiation are eliminated, no steady solution could be ob- tained. This suggests that for the two-dimensional adiabatic ﬂame (i.e., without radiative losses), either steady spread is not possi- ble (even for a thin solid) or the ﬂame is too long for the compu- tational domain. The resolution of this question depended on the development of an unsteady model. Using a two-dimensional transient model in low-speed forced ﬂow, the question of limiting length has been investigated for both thin and thick solids [47] . With gas and surface radiation included, the thin sample reaches steady spread as expected. The diffusion ﬂame over the thick sample lengthens initially, but the growth rate slows down with time. At the end of the computation, the ﬂame tip growth rate is four order of magnitudes smaller than its initial value. This suggests that the ﬂame (or pyrolysis) length asymptot- ically reaches a limit. Since there is no burnout for the assumed thick solid, the ﬂame reaches a stationary non-propagating state. Analysis of the heat ﬂuxes in the preheat zone shows that at the pyrolysis front, the net surface radiation loss balances with the convective input from the gas phase. Thus the net

text: that the ﬂame (or pyrolysis) length asymptot- ically reaches a limit. Since there is no burnout for the assumed thick solid, the ﬂame reaches a stationary non-propagating state. Analysis of the heat ﬂuxes in the preheat zone shows that at the pyrolysis front, the net surface radiation loss balances with the convective input from the gas phase. Thus the net heat ﬂux to the solid approaches zero, consistent with the result that the growth rate of the pyrolysis front was very small. This numerical exper- iment supports a previously-advanced argument that for a wide, thick solid to reach a limiting length, suﬃcient surface radiative loss is needed at the pyrolysis front to balance the convective heat input from the ﬂame [28] . For a narrow sample, the lateral mixing and cooling from ambient air through the edge of the ﬂame can be an additional or even dominant factor. For a thin solid, the numerical model predicted a faster pyrol- ysis front spread rate than that of the pyrolysis base, i.e. ﬂame length increase. However, the rate of pyrolysis front advance slows down as the ﬂame lengthens, and eventually a steady spread with a constant ﬂame length is reached. The ﬂow entrance length ef- fect is also signiﬁcant for a fuel which leaves behind an inert ma- terial after the ﬂame passes. As will be shown, a short entrance length affects the velocity at the ﬂame base, and this creates a ﬂame length overshoot that will be expounded upon later. While a number steady spread experiments over thin solids in both buoyant and forced ﬂows have been carried out, the possibil- ity of a nearly-stationary, non-growing ﬂame over a thick solid was seldom reported. There was one normal gravity experiment burn- ing several 120-cm-long wood samples having thicknesses ranging from 3.2 to 25.4 mm [48] . In the absence of externally applied ra- diation, the upward ﬂame stops growing before reaching the top of the sample, thus attaining a limiting length. In the absence of externally applied ra- diation, the upward ﬂame stops growing before reaching the top of the sample, thus attaining a limiting length. Because the de- crease of convection and the increasing inﬂuence of radiation, the possibility of reaching a limiting length is expected to be greater in lower-speed ﬂow in microgravity. However, that requires both a long test duration and a large enough sample to test this hypothe- sis. This is one objective of the present work. 2.1. Present experiment It is not possible on Earth to reproduce forced-ﬂow ﬂame spread in microgravity, low-velocity ﬂows. Although experiments have been conducted in such conditions in spacecraft (sounding rockets, Space shuttle, Mir Space Station, ISS), the sample sizes have been small. Consequently, there still are questions related to the nature of the ﬂame spread process when the scale of the ma- terial to be tested is relatively large, both in width and length, es- pecially since it is well established that sample width affects the spread rate in small samples, at least for upward ﬂame spread [28,29] . Concerning the sample length, there is the question of whether or not the pyrolysis length becomes constant for long samples and if a non-growing ﬂame in concurrent ﬂow in micro- gravity is possible. There is also the issue of the ﬂame becoming turbulent as the ﬂame spreads along a large sample and its effect on the ﬂame spread characteristics. A more sophisticated numeri- cal model could provide some clarity, but ultimately it would still need to be validated with long-duration, large-scale ﬂame spread experiments. In addition, there remains some uncertainty on the effects of low pressure ( ∼0.6 atm) and elevated oxygen concentra- tion ( ∼34%) environments [49] . These atmospheric conditions are referred to as Space Exploration Atmospheres (SEA) and are de- signed to reduce preparation time for space walks, while keeping the partial pressure of oxygen acceptable for human respiration. The Saﬃre experimental series presented herein was developed to provide the deﬁnitive experiments with

The progress of the pyrolysis front and pyrolysis base (burn- out) shown in Fig. 4 has similar characteristics to that observed in normal gravity with a different thin cotton textile [35] and a ﬁl- ter paper [36] . However, instead of a monotonic approach to steady state, Fig. 4 shows that there is an overshoot of the ﬂame or pyrol- ysis length which peaks at about 30 s. The overshoot region last for approximately 100 s before a quasi-steady 2 state is reached. This was initially a surprising result, but can be explained based on the entrance-ﬂow boundary layer effect [47,52] . Referring to the illus- tration in Fig. 1 (right), an upstream boundary layer develops over a thin solid if there is inert or fuel remaining after the ﬂame pas- sage, which is the case for the SIBAL fabric used in the Saﬃre-1 2 Here, “steady state” is qualiﬁed to acknowledge the fact that as the ﬂame moves downstream, it is in a gradually thickening boundary layer and sees a slowly chang- ing effective ﬂow velocity at the ﬂame base. experiment. Assuming a Blasius proﬁle, the boundary layer thick- ness increases very fast near the leading edge of the sample or the sample card (see Fig. 3 for the sample placement) but away from the leading edge, the growth of boundary layer is very gradual. De- tailed modeling [52] shows that the Saﬃre-1 ﬂame is expected to be inside the velocity boundary layer (also shown later in Fig. 11 ). At the start of the burn, the ﬂame is close to the entrance and sees a larger effective air velocity in the thin boundary layer, hence a large burning rate and a longer ﬂame result. When the ﬂame base moves downstream, the boundary layer growth

title: Flame spread: Effects of microgravity and scale
text: expected to be inside the velocity boundary layer (also shown later in Fig. 11 ). At the start of the burn, the ﬂame is close to the entrance and sees a larger effective air velocity in the thin boundary layer, hence a large burning rate and a longer ﬂame result. When the ﬂame base moves downstream, the boundary layer growth slow down and a quasi-steady spread with lower spread rate is found. Although the boundary layer effect has been observed in earlier work and is still under present investigation for ﬂame spread in opposed ﬂow [21,22,53,54] , its effect on concurrent ﬂame spread has sel- dom been mentioned. Part of the reason for this is due to the construction of the SIBAL fuel, which leaves behind an unburned solid after the ﬂame passes, and therefore maintains the boundary layer initiation point. A thin paper, in contrast, might completely be consumed so that the boundary layer never forms upstream of the burnout point. Still, the current results are important as they provide understanding of boundary layer effects on ﬂame spread for more general scenarios involving real materials that might be encountered in an actual ﬁre. With the ﬂame reaching a quasi-steady state suﬃciently down- stream of the entrance, the implication is that the ﬂow veloc- ity proﬁle at the ﬂame base changes slowly with spread dis- tance. In the quasi-steady region, the spread rate is 1.75 mm/s and the pyrolysis length is about 4 cm—a surprisingly short ﬂame given our experience with upward-spreading (concurrent- ﬂow) ﬂames on Earth [35, 36, e.g.]. Finally, there is a slight in- crease of pyrolysis length near the end of the experiment. The reason is unclear, although since the ﬂame is now near the end of the tunnel, local ﬂow acceleration may be occurring as the airstream begins to neck-down as it approaches the exit fans. Numerical model and computational results A transient three-dimensional model based on [11,55] is refor- mulated to simulate the Saﬃre-1 and Saﬃre-2 experiment. Using the actual tunnel dimensions and sample locations, high-ﬁdelity geometric simulations are conﬁgured. The physical model consists of the fully three-dimensional, transient Navier–Strokes equations of mass, momentum, energy and species conservation. One-step, second-order overall ﬁnite-rate Arrhenius kinetics are adopted for the gas-phase reaction. The gas radiation transfer equation is solved by an S-N discrete ordinate method with CO 2 and H 2 O as participating species. Radiation absorption coeﬃcients for the gas mixture are based on local Planck mean absorption coeﬃcient with a correction factor [56] . The emittance of the solid fuel varies with the local sample thickness according to formula given in [57] . These data were obtained from measurement using FTIR in an inte- grated sphere. Radiation has a large inﬂuence on the microgravity low-ﬂow-speed ﬂames, as elaborated later. In the solid fuel, heat conduction in all three dimensions is in- cluded in the energy conservation equation. Thermo-gravimetric analysis (TGA) data for the SIBAL fabric were used to deduce the pyrolysis kinetics [11] . A two-step decomposition model was for- mulated. In the ﬁrst and

Thermo-gravimetric analysis (TGA) data for the SIBAL fabric were used to deduce the pyrolysis kinetics [11] . A two-step decomposition model was for- mulated. In the ﬁrst and major step, 80% of the combustibles were evolved in the temperature range 30 0–40 0 °C, and the remaining 20% were evolved at higher temperature range from 400 to 675 °C. Another feature of the model is the resolution of the ﬂame sta- bilization zone near the pyrolysis base with small computational grids. As shown in Fig. 6 , the temperature gradients are very steep there. Since the ﬂame base moves, a grid distribution scheme was developed to follow the ﬂame and make most eﬃcient use of the ﬁner grid structure there [58] . The ﬂame radiative input which has comparable magnitude at the pyrolysis front, decreases slower than the convective ﬂux so that there is more heat input from ﬂame radiation than from con- vection. The linear increase of the spread rate with the ﬂow velocity conﬁrms the predicted trend from both analytical and numerical models [36,40] . The quenching of the ﬂame at low ﬂow velocities is also predicted in the model [40] . In low-speed ﬂow, oxygen supply is reduced and the ﬂame standoff increases. The reduced convection leads to a low-intensity ﬂame which ampliﬁes the radiative losses. The losses lower the ﬂame temperature and leads to ﬂame quenching. All other concurrent spread data also show that spread rate increases with airﬂow velocity. However, with just two data points in the Saﬃre tests, it cannot be fully proven that the relationship is linear for larger samples. The 1-cm spread rates are below the 2-cm data, as expected due to width effects on the spread rate [29,47,62] . But for the Saﬃre samples having widths of 40.6 and 5 cm, the spread rates are even slower. This seemingly unexpected result is due to the fact that the BASS tunnel was sub- stantially smaller than the tunnel used for the Saﬃre experiments. The smaller tunnel facilitated an effective ﬂow speed increase in the ﬂame because of hot gas expansion. Figure 13 also depicts the opposed-ﬂow spread rates. The 2- cm-width data have a dependence of the opposed ﬂame spread on air velocity ﬁrst increasing, reaching a peak at around 15 cm/s of airﬂow and then decreasing. This trend has been shown previ- ously [3,7,22] , and verify the predictions from theoretical models [3,51,53,63,64] . The ﬂame quenching at low ﬂow velocity is due to radiation heat losses and low oxygen diffusion to the ﬂame, and the ﬂame blow-off at large ﬂow velocities is caused by low Damköhler number effects on the ﬂame chemical kinetics. This trend can only be observed in microgravity because at normal gravity buoyancy prevents ﬂame spread testing at low forced ﬂow velocities [22] . The present 40.6 cm wide data were slightly below the 2-cm curve and seems to have a stronger dependence on the ﬂow velocity. Again,

The reduced velocity in the boundary layer that the ﬂame experiences at that location in comparison with that experienced by the smaller samples can be substantial. Comparing the concurrent and the opposed spread data for the 40.6-cm-width Saﬃre samples, it is clear that the concurrent ﬂame spread is faster (1.8 mm/s vs. 1.3 mm/s in 20 cm/s ﬂow; and 2.3 mm/s vs. 0.98 mm/s in 25 cm/s ﬂow). However, this may not always be the case. At suﬃciently low airﬂow, a crossover can occur, i.e. opposed spread becomes faster than concurrent spread [18,22,53] . Based on Fig. 13 , the crossover velocity appears to be around 15 cm/s. The boundary layer entrance ﬂow effect and the crossover phenomena amplify the difference between buoyant up- ward spread and concurrent spread in purely forced ﬂow. In buoy- ant spread, upward is always faster than downward, at least in Earth gravity.

Limiting length for a thick solid burning in concurrent ﬂow We have seen that spreading ﬂames in forced-concurrent ﬂow and in upward-buoyant ﬂow reach a limiting length. In the initial ﬂame growth phase, the ﬂame tip spreads faster than the ﬂame base initially but slows down as ﬂame lengthens. When the speed of the ﬂame base catches up with that of the ﬂame tip, a steady spread with a constant ﬂame length is reached. So steady spread is controlled by the movement of the ﬂame base. The ﬂame base moves when the burning sample can no longer generate enough pyrolyzate to support a gaseous ﬂame. This can occur when the solid completely burns out or when the pyrolysis rate is greatly re- duced by more complex pyrolysis kinetics such as those for a cot- ton sample. For the present SIBAL cotton-ﬁberglass sample, there is approximately 20% of the combustible left after the gas-phase ﬂame passes. But a slower surface smoldering reaction can follow. For thin solids, steady spread and associated limiting length are controlled by the ﬂame base movement, which has been loosely referred to as the sample ‘burnout’ process. The average heat ﬂux over the pyrolysis zone is thus important to determine the ﬂame length [60] . But, for short ﬂames in forced ﬂow, the spatial distri- butions of heat ﬂux and local burning rate are highly non-uniform. As demonstrated in Figs. 9 –11 , pyrolysis near the ﬂame base zone can dominate. From a theoretical point of view, resolving the struc- ture of this zone is crucial. If there is no sample burnout (or very slow burnout) such as the case with a suﬃciently thick solid, can a limiting length be reached? If so, this would be termed a nearly-stationary, non- growing ﬂame. As we mentioned in introduction, an earlier work [28] suggested this possibility by considering the heat balance in the preheat region. A transient numerical model [47] has also shown that radiative loss can balance convection in the down- stream region so that

text: solid, can a limiting length be reached? If so, this would be termed a nearly-stationary, non- growing ﬂame. As we mentioned in introduction, an earlier work [28] suggested this possibility by considering the heat balance in the preheat region. A transient numerical model [47] has also shown that radiative loss can balance convection in the down- stream region so that the pyrolysis tip spread rate asymptotes to zero (in the theoretical model, no solid burnout was assumed 3 ). To verify this possibility, we need a reasonably long and thick solid sample and suﬃcient test duration. Sample 9 from Saﬃre-2 ﬁts this requirement. Sample 9 is a 1-cm-thick cast PMMA sample measuring 5 cm (width) x 29 cm (length). The leading edge of the sample is slightly tapered to facilitate ignition. Flame occurs on both sides of the sample in the test. Figure 14 shows the time tracking of ﬂame tip and ﬂame base. The top-view ﬂame images are given in the inset. After an initial ﬂame length spike due to the igniter being on, the ﬂame tip re- treats to 1.2 cm and the ﬂame growth process starts. The tip speed slows down with time. The ﬂame tip approaches a limiting posi- tion after about 750 s. The test was terminated at 900 s (15 min). The ﬂame base starts a slow movement at ∼400 s. The movement is small and at 900 s, it is located at 5 mm. Note that the PMMA sample is tapered at the leading edge and PMMA may experience surface regression during the test duration. The limiting length is about 9 cm, slightly longer than those for the thin fabrics. Note that a previous microgravity experiment using a PMMA rod (0.476 cm radius) had a similar outcome, i.e. reaching a steady non-growing ﬂame. The ﬂame length increased nearly linearly with ﬂow velocity [66] . Limiting length is a function of many parameters including, ﬂow velocity, oxygen percentage, pressure and others. 6. Conclusions For the ﬁrst time, large-scale and long-duration ﬂame spread in microgravity was studied experimentally. This was enabled 3 By assuming a steady pyrolysis zone without radiation, a steady spread solution was obtained for a thick solid [65] . through a unique set of experiments conducted on an unmanned spacecraft while in orbit. Large fuel samples consisting of cotton- ﬁberglass fabric sheets were burned in a large ﬂow tunnel in two microgravity ﬂight experiments. Long-duration tests of a smaller fabric sample and a thick PMMA sample were also carried out in a separate mission. The main ﬁndings are: 1. A spreading ﬂame in forced-concurrent ﬂow in micrograv- ity can reach a quasi-steady state with a slow spread rate and a constant ﬂame length. In the present experiment, with a tunnel entrance ﬂow of 20–25 cm/s, the limiting pyrol- ysis lengths are about 4–5 cm and spread rate are around 2 mm/s. A numerical model suggests the importance of ra- diative losses for producing these short ﬂames. 2. In comparison, for the same fabric material, sample size, and atmosphere, upward spread is accelerating with increas- ing ﬂame length in normal gravity. Steady spread in normal gravity can be achieved only when excessive heat loss is in- troduced (e.g. by burning only on one side), in low pressure, or with narrow samples (for most materials). Even in such cases, steady spread in normal gravity has a much longer ﬂame and faster spread rate compared to microgravity. 3. The computed local solid burning rate varies drastically along the pyrolysis zone for short microgravity ﬂames, hav- ing a large peak close to the ﬂame base. This is also reﬂected in the measured surface temperature distribution. In con- trast, the surface temperature and presumably the burning rate are more uniform across the pyrolysis zone in upward spreading ﬂames. 4. In forced ﬂow, if a boundary layer develops

text: drastically along the pyrolysis zone for short microgravity ﬂames, hav- ing a large peak close to the ﬂame base. This is also reﬂected in the measured surface temperature distribution. In con- trast, the surface temperature and presumably the burning rate are more uniform across the pyrolysis zone in upward spreading ﬂames. 4. In forced ﬂow, if a boundary layer develops upstream of the ﬂame base, the effective ﬂow speed at the height of the con- current ﬂame can be lower than the imposed entrance ﬂow. This shortens the ﬂame and slows down the spread. How- ever, in the slowly-varying portion of the boundary layer away from its start, quasi-steady spread can be observed. 5. A long-duration experiment burning a thick PMMA sample shows that the ﬂame in microgravity asymptotically reaches a limiting length with minimum sample burnout at the ﬂame base. This lends support to previous arguments and numerical results regarding non-growing ﬂames over thick samples. 6. Flame spread and material ﬂammability in microgravity are affected by many other factors such as tunnel height, oxygen percentage, pressure, etc. Spacecraft ﬁre safety can beneﬁt by more fundamental research in these areas. title: Observations of Long Duration Microgravity Spherical Diffusion Flames Aboard the International Space Station
text: 1 Abstract: Spherical diffusion flames of gaseous fuels supported on a porous spherical burner are investigated experimentally in microgravity for long durations aboard the International Space Station (ISS). Experimental results are compared with a transient numerical model. The experiments involve normal spherical diffusion flames (i.e., fuel flowing into oxidizer) burning ethylene in an oxygen/nitrogen mixture at atmospheric pressure. The stoichiometric mixture fraction and adiabatic flame temperature are varied by diluting the fuel with nitrogen and varying the oxygen concentration in the ambient. The diagnostics consist of color video, thin-filament pyrometry for gas temperature, thermocouple measurements of burner surface temperature, and photomultiplier tube measurements of broad and narrow-band flame emission. Burn times range from 28 – 336 seconds. All flames grow monotonically after ignition. Peak gas temperature generally decreases with time. Radiative extinction is observed when, at constant reactant flow rate, the flame expands until radiation heat loss approaches the chemical heat release. Before a flame experiences complete extinction, it may enter an oscillatory mode in which part of the flame partially extinguishes and then reforms. The oscillations grow in magnitude until complete extinction. Sufficiently small flames with low radiation losses exhibit quasi-steady behavior, but burner heating is significant, and the experimental duration is dictated by the temperature limit of the porous sphere. Keywords: Ethylene; Oscillatory extinction; Radiative extinction; Spherically-symmetric diffusion flames; Thin-filament pyrometry

title: Observations of Long Duration Microgravity Spherical Diffusion Flames Aboard the International Space Station
text: 2 1 Introduction Diffusion flames in microgravity have important implications for spacecraft fire safety and also offer a unique opportunity to study fundamental combustion phenomena in a buoyancy free environment. Gaseous burner-supported spherical diffusion flames in microgravity are particularly interesting, owing to their intrinsic one-dimensional structure, controllable reactant flow rate, and diffusion dominated transport. To date, owing to limitations on the duration of microgravity attainable, no experiments have been conducted to investigate burner-supported spherical diffusion flames in long-duration microgravity. Several spherical flame configurations have been studied in microgravity, including droplet flames [1-5], candle flames [6], and gaseous burner-supported spherical flames [7-15]. Droplet flames, however, have a fuel supply that is uncontrollable, as the vaporization rate (i.e., the fuel flow rate) is an eigenvalue of the one-dimensional problem. Additionally, the fuel concentration and the direction of convection relative to the flame cannot be varied (it is always from the fuel to the oxidizer). Candle flames suffer from similar limitations. Additionally, candle flames only have a spherically symmetric flow field at the tip of the wick. A steady solution does not exist for cylindrical flow (as induced over the length of the wick), thus the resulting flame is a hemispherical cap, which can behave quite differently from a sphere. Gaseous burner-supported spherical diffusion flames, on the other hand, offer a controllable reactant flow rate, the ability to control the concentration of the fuel supply, and the ability to operate such that the direction of convection across the flame can be from the fuel to the oxidizer or the oxidizer to the fuel, making them ideal for fundamental studies of microgravity spherical diffusion flames.

title: Observations of Long Duration Microgravity Spherical Diffusion Flames Aboard the International Space Station
text: 3 The absence of buoyancy in microgravity, coupled with the inverse-square dependence of reactant velocity on radius in a spherical configuration, results in substantially longer time scales for microgravity spherical diffusion flames to fully develop. To observe and investigate the development of a microgravity spherical diffusion flame, an adequate duration of microgravity must be available. Previous gaseous microgravity spherical diffusion flame investigations have been limited by experimental conditions in terrestrial drop towers, which allow for only 2-5 seconds of microgravity [7,9-13,15]. During these short times, the flame either continues to grow, or extinguishes. Owing to this intrinsic time limitation, studies of gaseous spherical diffusion flames have largely focused on extinction. In NASA’s 2.2 Second Drop Tower, Chernovsky et al. [11,15] measured transient temperature and radiation intensity in ethylene spherical diffusion flames for varying diluents on both the fuel and oxidizer side of the flame. They numerically predicted flame extinction, but never achieved it experimentally. Tse et al. [7] also used the 2.2 Second Drop Tower to study the transient response of spherical flames in microgravity but did not observe extinction experimentally. Santa et al. [12,13] used the 2.2 Second Drop Tower and examined radiative extinction in ethylene spherical diffusion flames. Extinction was only observed in flames with a heavily diluted ambient. The above referenced drop tower studies have found that spherical flames in microgravity continue to grow until either extinction, or the end the experimental duration [7,11,12,13,15]. Tse et al. [7] attributed this growth to fuel vapor accumulation. Many researchers suggest that as the flame grows, radiative losses increase until they become comparable to the chemical heat release and the flame extinguishes (i.e., radiative extinction) [12,13,16-20].

title: Observations of Long Duration Microgravity Spherical Diffusion Flames Aboard the International Space Station
text: 4 Figure 1 illustrates the theoretical temporal behavior of flame radius for a spherical diffusion flame in microgravity. These curves are solutions of gaseous spherical diffusion flames without radiation for three burner reactant flow rates [21]. Similar to drop tower observations, Fig. 1 shows that spherical diffusion flames in microgravity grow monotonically. The relative size of a spherical diffusion flame increases with increasing burner reactant flow rate, or with decreasing ambient reactant concentration. The location of extinction in Fig. 1 is arbitrary and is included to illustrate the radiative extinction seen in drop towers, where flames have grown such that radiative losses approach the chemical heat release of the flame, causing the flame to extinguish. This study aims to investigate the dynamics of a spherical diffusion flame in long duration microgravity. By conducting experiments on the International Space Station (ISS), we have ample time in microgravity to observe fully-developed spherical diffusion flames. Experimental results are compared with a numerical simulation. This investigation was conducted under the experiment Flame Design, which is one of six experiments in the NASA project, Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME). 2 Experimental 2.1 Experimental Hardware Experiments are performed in microgravity aboard the International Space Station (ISS) in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR). Only normal flames (i.e., fuel issuing from the porous spherical burner into an ambient oxidizer) have been investigated thus far. The fuel is ethylene (C2H4), the diluent is nitrogen (N2), and the oxidizer is an oxygen (O2)/N2 mixture. The ambient oxidizer is limited to 40% O2 owing to safety concerns. Quiescent ambient conditions, with the

title: Observations of Long Duration Microgravity Spherical Diffusion Flames Aboard the International Space Station
text: 5 oxidizer at 295K, are established in a 105 L chamber with a free volume of 83.4 L. Pressure can be varied from approximately 0.5 to 1.5 bar but is 1 bar in this work. Figure 2 illustrates the experimental configuration and a spherical diffusion flame. The burner is a 6.4 mm diameter porous stainless steel sphere. Fuel is supplied to the burner via a 1.17/1.5 mm (inside/outside diameter) tube. Because this tube was found to be physically weak, it was encased in a larger 1.6/1.83 mm (inside/outside diameter) support tube to avoid damage to the fuel supply tube during assembly. The reactant supplied to the burner is either ethylene or ethylene diluted with nitrogen. Reactant flow rates are controlled with mass flow controllers with an estimated uncertainty of ± 5%. Ignition is achieved using a hot wire igniter that retracts after ignition. At the beginning of each test day, the chamber is filled to the desired pressure and oxidizer concentration. The oxygen concentration decreases marginally during the test day as the oxygen is consumed by combustion. In between experiments, a mixing fan is used to ensure a homogenous chamber environment for the next test. Combustion products (e.g., CO2 and H2O) are occasionally scrubbed from the chamber to remove excess radiators and to prevent condensation on the chamber walls and optical windows. Color images of the flames are obtained using the ACME data camera, a 1.4-megapixel color camera with a charge-coupled device (CCD) sensor. The lens on the ACME data camera is motorized and allows control over zoom, focus, and iris. The camera gain is also variable. Its framing rate is generally slow owing to exposure optimization and data limits on the ISS. The tests are also recorded at 30 frames per second (fps) using the ACME operations camera, a 0.44- megapixel CCD color video camera. Images of CH* emission are captured at 23 fps using a

title: Observations of Long Duration Microgravity Spherical Diffusion Flames Aboard the International Space Station
text: 6 monochrome intensified camera. The magnifications of all three cameras were determined prior to launch and were confirmed from the porous sphere images during each ISS test. The flame radius as a function of time is measured using the ACME operations camera video. Still images are extracted from the video and an ellipse is fit where the intensities are approximately midway between the peak blue and the ambient intensities (i.e., approximately the region of stoichiometry [22]). The flame radius is taken as the radius of the ellipse perpendicular to the fuel supply tube because the flame is quenched at the burner support tube, making it difficult to determine the location of the flame sheet parallel to the burner tube. Additionally, the flame is shifted somewhat towards the burner support tube (i.e., the flame is spherical, but no longer concentric with the porous sphere). This is likely owing to either reactant leakage where the fuel supply tube connects to the porous sphere, or to the lower temperature (and subsequently lower diffusivity) in the quenched region. Uncertainties in the flame radii are estimated at ± 0.3 mm. Spectral irradiance is measured with three photomultiplier tubes (PMTs). One is unfiltered and detects 230 – 700 nm. The other two have bandpass filters at wavelengths corresponding to CH* (431 nm) and OH* (310 nm). Burner temperature is measured using a sheathed 0.25 mm diameter type-K thermocouple attached to the burner surface. 2.2 Thin-filament pyrometry Thin-filament pyrometry [23,24], or TFP, is performed using 14 μm SiC fibers [25] to determine the peak gas-phase temperature as a function of time. The fibers are initially straight and in the image plane of the camera, but they can expand slightly upon heating. Temperatures are

title: Observations of Long Duration Microgravity Spherical Diffusion Flames Aboard the International Space Station
text: 7 determined using intensities from the three colors (i.e., wavelength bands) of the camera’s color filter array (CFA): red (R), green (G), and blue (B). The ACME data camera has a linear response with exposure time [25,26]. The camera was calibrated using a blackbody calibration source. Blackbody images were captured from 1073 to 1473 K in 50 K increments. Camera settings are adjusted at each blackbody temperature such that the images are just below saturation. The blackbody images were recorded in RAW format and converted to 16-bit TIFF files using ImageJ. The images are demosaiced in MATLAB. For each blackbody image, the mean intensity for the R, G, and B colors is found for a 10 × 10 pixel region at the center of the area of signal. Nearly identical results are obtained using G. The B pixel intensities are too low to be used. An attempt was made to use two-color ratio TFP pyrometry [27], but the color ratio curves obtained from the blackbody calibration for this camera are multi-valued in this temperature range and thus cannot be used. For TFP aboard the ISS, the exposure time is 0.4 s and there is a delay of 75 ms between images. The f-number is between 3.8 and 10.2. The diagonal field of view varies between 69 and 80 mm. The blackbody furnace used for the camera calibration is large enough that the signal intensity is spread over a large number of pixels. the SiC fiber diameter, however, is smaller than the camera resolution and the camera is intentionally defocused to illuminate a sufficient number of pixels. To account for the fiber width in the image plane, a fill factor is introduced, defined as the unheated fiber’s width in the image divided by the width of a pixel. The fill factors here are between 0.3 and 0.35, depending on the zoom. Fiber images are recorded in HOBJ format and converted to 16-bit color TIFF files using OMA2 [28]. For each column of pixels (i.e., the radial direction of the fiber), pixel intensities from just above and below the fiber’s luminescence are identified as the local background. These are averaged and subtracted from the intensity of each pixel in the column. The R pixel intensities for each column are then averaged. Each average is divided by the fiber fill factor. This process is repeated for each column crossing the glowing fiber. This identifies two local TFP maxima,

To account for this, the determined NI is divided by a transmissivity factor of 0.36, chosen to approximately match the simulated temperatures below. title: Observations of Long Duration Microgravity Spherical Diffusion Flames Aboard the International Space Station
text: 10 Microgravity experiments, particularly on the ISS, have been proven to be challenging. Once the experimental apparatuses are launched, they generally cannot be altered or repaired, and the effects of space (e.g., cosmic rays) on the diagnostics are unknown. Additionally, diagnostic calibrations must be done on Earth prior to launch and they cannot be recalibrated. Nonetheless, while it is difficult to acquire quantitative data on the ISS, the available diagnostics do provide valuable semi-quantitative data under conditions unattainable on earth. 3. Numerical Model Numerical simulations were performed using the SphDiff program used in refs. [12,13,29,30], which is a modification of Sandia PREMIX [31]. The governing equations are discretized using finite differencing methods and the model uses a modified Newton method to solve the discretized equations. Radiation losses are calculated using a detailed absorption/emission statistical narrow band model with wavenumbers ranging from 150 – 9300 cm-1, coupled with a discrete-ordinates method with 20 ordinates. A detailed description of both methods is found in ref. [32]. Radiation from and reabsorption by CO, CO2 and H2O are included. Conservation of species and energy are the same as ref. [32]. To improve numerical stability, conservation of mass was replaced by this version of the ideal-gas equation [14]: , (4) where ρ is density, t is time, T is temperature, MW is the mixture molar mass, MWk is the molar mass of species k, Y is mass fraction, and KK is the total number of species. Pressure does not appear in Eq. (4) because it is assumed constant.

text: 11 The computational domain extends from 0.32 cm at the burner surface to 100 cm at the outer boundary. The detailed boundary conditions for each equation are shown in ref. [32] unless noted otherwise. Burner heating has a second order effect on the results, but is non-negligible; thus, the inner boundary temperature was set to the experimentally measured burner temperature. There was no detectable change in species or temperature at the outer boundary, indicating that the size of the domain is sufficiently large. The grid algorithm has been slightly modified. At the beginning of each time step, the center of the reaction zone was identified as the location of maximum temperature. The mesh was then adapted to assign the smallest grid spacing there. The gridding algorithm is such that the domain is divided into three zones: an inner zone, a reaction zone, and an outer zone. The inner zone follows the same algorithm as Ref. [32]. The reaction zone has 200 nodes with 0.001 cm grid spacing. The grid spacing in the outer zone increases by 5% for each grid cell moving outward. A total of 400 grid points was used, which was found to satisfy grid independence. For this paper, a UCSD mechanism with 57 species and 259 reaction steps was used to simulate the flames [33]. Unlike previous studies [12,13,14,32], which simulate flames for 2.2 seconds (i.e., drop tower studies), flames in this investigation are simulated for up to 336 second. The UCSD mechanism keeps the number of species and reactions small for numerical tractability and uncertainty reduction introduced by reaction rates. 4. Results & Discussion Based on experimental observations (e.g., drop tower and ISS tests) and Fig. 1, microgravity spherical diffusion flames grow monotonically with time. The increasing flame diameter and accumulation of product gases (primarily CO2 and H2O) result in an increase in

title: Observations of Long Duration Microgravity Spherical Diffusion Flames Aboard the International Space Station
text: 12 radiative heat losses and decreased peak temperatures. Simultaneously, as the flame diameter increases, the rate of chemical heat release at the flame may decrease, owing to the decreasing diffusion rate to the flame. Eventually the flame may grow until radiative heat losses are comparable to the chemical heat release, resulting in radiative extinction [12]. The relative radius of a normal spherical diffusion flame in microgravity generally increases with increasing fuel flow rate, and with decreasing oxygen concentration in the ambient. These observations suggest that the key to achieving long duration spherical diffusion flames in microgravity is to minimize radiative heat loss by using low fuel flow rates and/or relatively high ambient oxygen concentrations to yield small flames. Table 1 summarizes the experimental conditions of the four long duration spherical flames examined herein. Each test has a unique reactant flow rate, stoichiometric mixture fraction (Zst), and adiabatic flame temperature. Zst is described in detail in refs. [9,10]. The quantity, XO2, is the ambient oxygen concentration, whose uncertainty is estimated to be ±0.004. Each flame has a relatively low fuel flow rate to facilitate long experimental duration. Figure 4 shows a representative image of each flame. All flames reported here contained no luminosity from soot after the ignition transient. Thus, radiation from soot is not considered in the numerical simulations. The flames are reasonably spherical, but not concentric with the porous sphere, and local flame quenching is apparent near the fuel supply tube. The image for flame 2 is Table 1. text: 13 from the ACME data camera, while those for flames 1, 3, and 4 are from the monochrome intensified camera with a CH* filter, owing to the weak flame luminosity. The CH* images were false colored to simulate the color of the flame. Figure 5 shows experimental measurements and numerical predictions of flame radius. Measured burner temperatures are also shown. Owing to the low fuel flow rates and subsequently small flames, burner heating is significant. Fig. 5 shows that the rate of increase of the burner temperature is coupled to the size of the flame (i.e., smaller flames cause the burner to heat up more rapidly). However, burner heating is also a function of the fuel concentration (i.e., Zst), inlet gas temperature, and burner material properties. While burner heating is significant, it has been shown that flame size is primarily a function of the reactant flow rate and the properties of the oxidizer side [15,20]. Because the effect of burner temperature on flame size is second order, the experimental burner temperature is used as a boundary condition in the numerical model. To illustrate the effect of burner heating, the dotted curve for flame 2 (the flame with the most significant burner heating) in Fig. 5 denotes the numerical prediction when the burner temperature is held constant at 300 K. When the burner temperature is held constant at 300 K, the flame size changes by less than 5%. Owing to material limitations, the burner temperature was not allowed to exceed 773K (500 °C), a limit that was only met for flame 2. Flames 1 and 4 extinguished when the flow was terminated, and flame 3 extinguished radiatively. The burner temperature for flames 3 and 4 reached a peak and then decreased slowly, indicating that the flame is moving farther from the burner and/or cooling. The burner temperature for flames 1 and 2 is still increasing at the end of the test.

text: 14 The numerical predictions of flame radius in Fig. 5 show excellent agreement with the experimental measurements. The first 10 s for flames 3 and 4 is excluded to better depict the behavior of the other flames. Flame 1 shows a peak flame radius at approximately 5 s. This flame was ignited at a fuel flow rate slightly higher than the test condition to facilitate ignition. The fuel flow rate was then ramped down to the test condition. The numerical model accounted for this and was able to accurately capture the behavior. The vertical dashed line shown for flame 3 indicates the onset of flame oscillations in which a portion of the flame continuously extinguishes and reforms, growing in magnitude with time until complete extinction. text: 16 Table 2 shows the calculated quasi-steady flame radii for the flames in Table 1. The calculated flame radii accurately capture the trends observed in Fig. 5. As observed in previous investigations, these spherical diffusion flames in microgravity grow monotonically with time, even in long duration. However, they do exhibit an asymptotic trend, with the rate of growth decreasing with time. Flame 3 asymptotes to conditions that lead to extinction. It is unclear if flames 1, 2, and 4 would asymptote to flammable conditions. The burner temperature of flame 4 is decreasing, which could be due to the increasing flame radius and/or decreasing flame temperature, either of which may lead to extinction. Figure 6 shows the experimentally measured OH* and unfiltered (230-700 nm) irradiance. All three PMTs (OH*, CH*, and unfiltered) show similar trends of flame irradiance with time, thus CH* emission is not included. If the flame is approaching extinction, the intensity measured by the PMT will decrease and go to zero when the flame extinguishes. The discontinuity in the unfiltered emission for flames 1, 3, and 4 is due to luminosity from the TFP fibers entering the flames. The fiber insertion in flame 1 is less apparent owing to the simultaneous flowrate change. The irradiance from flame 3 gradually decreases until it enters the oscillatory mode. The oscillations grow in magnitude with time until the flame extinguishes, and the irradiance then goes to zero. The emissions for flame 4 show an asymptotic trend, and for flames 1 and 2 appear steady, Table 2. Theoretical quasi-steady flame size. Flame Flame Radius [mm] 1 9.0 2 7.7 3 14.3 4 14.9

text: 17 or slightly increasing. The slight increase in irradiance is likely due to the increasing flame radius, increasing flame temperature, and/or the rapidly increasing burner temperature. The oscillatory mode of flame 3 is illustrated in Fig. 7. Figure 7a show the progression of one full oscillation as a portion of the flame extinguishes and then reforms. The oscillations continue to grow until complete extinction, as seen in Fig. 7b. The OH* irradiance in Fig. 7b is magnified in Fig. 7c to better illustrate the dynamics of one full oscillation. The exact time interval for the photos of Fig. 7a is denoted with red vertical dashed lines in Fig. 7c. A similar oscillatory phenomenon has been observed in microgravity candle flames [6] and droplet flames [1,2,35]. The oscillations seen herein begin near the fuel supply tube (i.e., region where the flame is quenched) and progress towards the opposite side of the porous sphere (i.e., the region of highest reactivity and temperature). The region opposite of the fuel supply tube is also the thinnest and brightest part of the flame (see Fig. 4), suggesting that this region has the lowest radiative losses. The oscillatory mode is likely induced by the quenched region at the burner tube, and the growth in the oscillations, and ultimately extinction, is due to the decreasing flame temperature as the flame grows and radiation heat loss increases. The oscillatory mode referenced herein will be further addressed in a future manuscript. Figure 8 shows the simulated and experimentally measured peak gas temperatures (i.e., flame temperatures) as functions of time. There is no TFP data for flame 2. The experimental peak temperatures show good agreement with the simulated peak temperatures, particularly the trends with time. For flame 1, the experimental flame temperature measurements are roughly 150 K lower than the numerical predictions. The cause of this is under investigation. Uncertainty could be associated with the change in flow rate during this test. It should be noted that this discrepancy

title: Observations of Long Duration Microgravity Spherical Diffusion Flames Aboard the International Space Station
text: 18 would not have a large effect on flame size, because flame size is primarily a function of reactant flow rate and the properties of the oxidizer side [15,20,36]. Experimental flame temperature measurements are taken for flame 3, even during the oscillatory phenomenon, due to the thin-filament fiber always being in a location where the flame exists, as seen in Fig. 7a. The measured and simulated flame temperatures show that the flame temperature asymptotes until the flame extinguishes at a measured temperature of 1140 K after 337 s, and a simulated temperature of 1135 K after 335 s. These extinction temperatures are similar to the extinction temperature of ethylene seen in other spherical flame investigations (approximately 1150 K) [12]. The flame temperature of flame 4 is also temporally asymptotic, but it is unclear if the flame would extinguish at long times. The flame temperatures for flames 1 and 2 are relatively constant, or increasing slightly, after the ignition transient. This increase is due to the rapidly increasing temperature of the burner and the convection of heat to the flame. This assumption has been verified by running the numerical simulation assuming a constant burner temperature of 300 K. The result is denoted by the dashed line for flame 2 in Fig. 8. When the surface of the burner is maintained at 300 K, the flame temperature for flames 1 and 2 decreases asymptotically with time, similar to flames 3 and 4. 5. Conclusions Long duration gaseous spherical microgravity diffusion flames aboard the International Space Station (ISS) were examined. Experimental results were compared with simulations from a transient numerical model. The following observations were made:

title: Observations of Long Duration Microgravity Spherical Diffusion Flames Aboard the International Space Station
text: 19 1) Long duration burner-supported microgravity spherical diffusion flames grow monotonically with time. The rate of growth decreases with time as the flames asymptotically approach a condition that may never be reached, owing to extinction. 2) Burner heating is intrinsically coupled to flame radius for small flames near the burner but has a second order effect on flame size. Significant burner heating in very small flames can cause the flame temperature to increase with time by convection of heat to the flame, but the flame continues to grow with time. After reaching a peak, the burner temperature may decrease with time owing to the flame moving farther from the burner and/or decreasing flame temperature. 3) As flames approach extinction, they may enter an unstable oscillatory mode in which they partially extinguish and reform. The oscillations grow in magnitude with time until complete flame extinction. The oscillations begin at the region the quenched flame near the fuel supply tube and progress towards the region of highest temperature (i.e., the region opposite the fuel supply tube). 4) For modest fuel flow rates (modest flame radii), the flame temperature typically decreases with time due to increasing flame radius and the subsequent increase in radiative heat loss. In such flames, the flame temperature asymptotically approaches a temperature that may or may not lead to extinction. For low fuel flow rates (small flames) the flame temperature remains relatively constant, or increases, due to heat convected to the flame from the burner. 5) Measurements of radiant emissions in the visible and UV show that flames with decreasing peak gas temperature exhibit asymptotically decreasing irradiance. Flames with increasing or nearly constant peak gas temperature exhibit increasing or constant irradiance. This effort to study burner stabilized spherical diffusion flames on the ISS has revealed the basic characteristic of these flames. Based on the results herein, the general question whether there

title: Observations of Long Duration Microgravity Spherical Diffusion Flames Aboard the International Space Station
text: 20 is a steady-state condition for burner-supported spherical diffusion flames remains unanswered. Future studies are being conducted to further understand the fundamental characteristics of long- duration microgravity spherical diffusion flames (e.g., radiative extinction, the existence of a steady-state spherical diffusion flame, soot formation, and the impact of stoichiometric mixture fraction). An investigation of inverse microgravity spherical flames (i.e., where oxidizer issues from the burner into an environment of fuel) will also be conducted aboard the ISS. title: Dynamics of Cool Flames
text: 1 Dynamics of Cool Flames Yiguang Jua, Christopher B. Reutera, Omar R. Yehiaa, Tanvir I. Faroukb, and Sang Hee Wonb a Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544, USA bDepartment of Mechanical Engineering, University of South Carolina, SC 29208, USA Summary Cool flames play a critical role in ignition timing, burning rate, burning limits, engine knocking, and emissions in conventional and advanced combustion engines. This paper provides an overview of the recent progress in experimental and computational studies of cool flames. First, a brief review of low-temperature chemistry and classical studies of cool flames is presented. Next, the recent experimental and computational findings of cool flames in microchannels, microgravity droplet combustion, counterflow flames, and turbulent combustion environments are reviewed. The flammability diagrams of different low-temperature flames and their relations to hot flames in premixed and nonpremixed systems are discussed. The impact of cool flames on turbulent combustion and knock formation is also highlighted. Finally, future avenues in cool flame research, including the use of cool flames as a new platform for low-temperature kinetic model validation, are presented. It is concluded that the understanding and control of low- temperature combustion is critical for the development of future advanced engines and new fuels. Key words: Cool flame, low-temperature chemistry, flame dynamics © 2019 published by Elsevier. Introduction The study of cool flames has entered its third century [1-5], and the understanding of their structure and dynamics has evolved with advancing kinetic understanding and experimental, diagnostic, and computational methods. Due to recent developments in alternative fuels and advanced engine designs [6-14] as well as the recent discovery of transient nonpremixed cool flames in microgravity droplet combustion in space [15] and self-sustaining cool flames in counterflow burners [16, 17], research interest in cool flames is at a high point. Experimental and computational advances in cool flame research have been made in a number of areas and have led to new observations of nonpremixed and premixed warm flames [18-21]. These advances have provided new platforms to understand the dynamics and chemistry of low-temperature flames and assess their impact on new fuels and future engine design. 1.1 Motivations for cool flame research In order to reduce emissions and improve fuel efficiency in engines, high-pressure and low- temperature combustion strategies such as homogenous charge compression ignition (HCCI) [7, 8, 22], reactivity controlled compression ignition (RCCI) [8], partially premixed compression ignition (PPCI) [23-25], advanced compression ignition (ACI), and spark-assisted compression ignition (SACI) have attracted great attention [26, 27]. In traditional gasoline and diesel engines, combustion is dominated by transport-controlled high-temperature premixed flames and nonpremixed flames, respectively. However, in HCCI, RCCI, PPCI, ACI, and SACI engines, autoignition and cool flames play a critical role in fuel consumption and heat release rate (HRR) due to partial or complete fuel and air premixing at a higher engine pressures, as seen in Fig. 1 for PPCI.
